items.subtype_name: Set up a belief, then knock it down
items.stimulus: Linguists long assumed that young children learn new words mainly when an adult points to an object and names it for them. A study by linguist Dana Okafor, however, complicates that view. Okafor had toddlers watch two adults talk to each other. One adult used an unfamiliar word for a toy, and neither adult ever spoke to the child. Later, most of the toddlers correctly chose the toy the word referred to. This suggests that children also learn vocabulary from conversations they only overhear.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To describe how a conversation between two adults was staged for a group of toddlers
To challenge the assumption that children learn new words mainly through direct naming
To argue that children learn no words when adults point to objects and name them
To confirm the view that direct naming is how children learn nearly all new words
items.explanation: The text opens with what linguists 'long assumed', and then 'however' signals doubt. The study shows toddlers learning a word they only overheard, which is evidence against the idea that children learn words mainly through direct naming. The text's purpose is to challenge that assumption.

A.why: You described what most of the text contains, the staged conversation, instead of what the text is for. The study is there as evidence against the old belief.

C.why: You went too far. The text says children 'also' learn from overheard speech. It never says direct naming teaches them nothing.

D.why: You missed the 'however'. The text questions the naming view. It does not confirm it.

items.subtype_name: Set up a belief, then knock it down
items.stimulus: Folklorists have often compared oral storytelling to a game of telephone, in which a tale drifts further from its original with every retelling. Yet folklorist Ilse Marten found a striking counterexample. A riddle tale written down in a coastal Norwegian parish in 1790 closely matches a version Marten recorded from a storyteller in the same parish in 2015. The two share nearly every plot event and even several exact phrases. Oral tradition, it seems, can preserve a story with surprising precision.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To trace the plot events of a riddle tale told in a coastal Norwegian parish
To claim that orally transmitted tales never change as they pass between tellers
To question the view that orally transmitted tales inevitably drift from their originals
To support the idea that tales become less accurate with each new retelling
items.explanation: The first sentence gives a common belief, the 'game of telephone' view. 'Yet' introduces a case that cuts against it: a tale that stayed almost the same for more than two centuries. The text exists to question the idea that oral tales always drift.

A.why: You picked what the example is about rather than why it is there. The riddle tale is evidence against a belief, and the text never traces its plot.

B.why: You turned one counterexample into an absolute rule. The text says oral tradition 'can' preserve stories, not that tales never change.

D.why: You chose the belief the text argues against. 'Yet' shows the author doubts the drift view.

items.subtype_name: Set up a belief, then knock it down
items.stimulus: Marine biologists have generally regarded sea cucumbers as minor members of coral reef communities, slow animals that do little more than drift across the seafloor. Recent fieldwork by Rafael Ibarra's team suggests otherwise. On a reef where sea cucumbers had been heavily harvested, the sediment held far less oxygen than on a nearby reef where they remained plentiful. To argue that sea cucumbers matter more to reef health than any other reef animal

To challenge the assumption that sea cucumbers contribute little to coral reef health

To describe how a historian gathered and examined a set of eighteenth-century maps

To show that most eighteenth-century maps filled their interiors with invented towns

items.stimulus: Materials scientists have generally treated graphene as a filler whose benefits scale with quantity: the more flakes mixed into a polymer, the stiffer the resulting composite. A 2025 study by Ana Oduya's team suggests that picture is incomplete. In epoxy samples, stiffness rose steadily up to about 1 percent graphene by weight, then flattened and even dipped as the flakes clumped into stacks that slid past one another. items.explanation: The belief here is the coaches' warning against stretching. Okafor shows that the evidence for it used unusually long holds with no warm-up. Under normal conditions she found no slowdown. The text questions the warning's basis but doesn't claim stretching helps. Choice D stays within what the text shows.

A.why: You flipped the warning into its opposite. Okafor's stretchers ran 'no slower', which is not the same as faster. The text never says stretching improves speed.

B.why: You got the direction backward. The earlier studies used holds that were longer than usual, a minute or more, not shorter.

C.why: The text never compares static stretching with dynamic warm-ups. Both groups' conditions are details of Okafor's trial, which is there to test the coaches' warning.
